items.title: SKILL.md — the whole format
items.summary: A folder, a markdown file, YAML frontmatter. That's the entire spec.
items.detail:
name and description in frontmatter, instructions in the body, optional scripts and reference files alongside. The description is the important line: it's what the agent reads to decide whether to load the skill at all, so it must say both what the skill does and when to use it.

User skills live in ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, project skills in .claude/skills/.
items.snippet:
---
name: pdf-report
description: Generate a branded PDF report from a CSV. Use when someone asks for a report, export, or client-ready PDF from tabular data.
---

## Steps
1. Validate the CSV columns
2. Render with scripts/render.py
3. Save to reports/

items.title: Progressive disclosure
items.summary: Only the description is always loaded — the body loads on demand. Design for that.
items.detail:
Skill descriptions sit in context permanently; bodies are read only when the skill fires. So: keep the frontmatter tight, push long procedures and reference tables into separate files the body links to, and you can have fifty skills installed without drowning the context window.

This is the single design principle that separates skills that scale from skills that bloat.
items.snippet:
SKILL.md          ← loaded when triggered
  references/api.md   ← loaded only if needed
  scripts/run.py      ← executed, never read into context

items.title: Write the description for the trigger, not the reader
items.summary: The #1 reason a skill never fires: a description that describes, instead of matching.
items.detail:
Include the words users will actually type, including the wrong ones. 'Use when the user says roast my pitch, review this press release, or is this any good' fires reliably; 'Provides feedback on PR materials' does not.

Third person, concrete triggers, and explicit non-triggers if the skill keeps firing when it shouldn't.
items.snippet:
description: >
  Roast a pitch or press release with a veteran PR director's eye.
  Use when the user says "roast my draft", "is this any good",
  asks for a pitch critique, or pastes PR copy wanting honest feedback.

items.title: Skill vs slash command vs subagent
items.summary: Three ways to package behaviour. Picking wrong is why your setup feels messy.
items.detail:
Slash command: you invoke it explicitly, it's a prompt template. Skill: the agent invokes it when the situation matches, it's a capability. Subagent: separate context window and tool set, it's a delegate.

Rule of thumb — if you'd type it, make it a command; if the agent should know to reach for it, make it a skill; if it would flood your context, make it a subagent.
items.snippet:
/command   you decide, prompt template
skill      agent decides, capability
subagent   separate context, delegate

items.title: Ship scripts, not instructions, for deterministic work
items.summary: If a step must happen the same way every time, it's code — not a bullet point.
items.detail: Anything deterministic (validation, file conversion, API calls with a fixed shape) belongs in a script the skill executes. Prose instructions get interpreted; scripts get run. Bonus: the script's output never enters context unless you print it.
items.snippet:
## Steps
1. Run `scripts/validate.py <file>` — it exits non-zero on bad input
2. Only if it passes, continue to the writing step

items.title: allowed-tools in frontmatter
items.summary: Bound a skill's blast radius at the skill level, not the session level.
items.detail: A research skill that only needs Read, Grep and WebFetch shouldn't be able to run Bash. Declaring tools in the skill's frontmatter means installing it doesn't widen what a session can do — which is what makes sharing skills across a team tolerable.
items.snippet:
---
name: dep-audit
description: Audit dependencies for known issues. Use when asked about vulnerable or outdated packages.
allowed-tools: Read, Grep, WebFetch
---

items.title: Use skill-creator to write skills
items.summary: The bundled meta-skill that scaffolds, structures and sanity-checks a new skill.
items.detail: It knows the format constraints, the description conventions and the progressive-disclosure layout — so your first skill doesn't have to be the one you learn the rules on. Describe the workflow you keep repeating by hand and let it produce the folder.
items.snippet: Use skill-creator to build a skill from this workflow I keep doing manually: [describe it]

items.title: Plugins are how skills travel
items.summary: Bundle skills, commands, agents, hooks and MCP servers into one installable unit.
items.detail: A plugin is the distribution format: a marketplace entry your team installs once to get the same commands, skills and tool connections. The right move when 'here's my dotfiles, copy these folders' stops scaling past three people.

items.title: One skill, one job
items.summary: A skill that does four things fires for none of them reliably.
items.detail: Trigger matching works on the description; four jobs means a fuzzy description means unpredictable firing. Split them, and let one skill reference another by name in its body if they genuinely chain.
items.snippet:
✗ pr-tools: writes pitches, finds journalists, checks facts, builds lists
✓ pitch-writer · journalist-finder · fact-check · media-list

items.title: Test the trigger, not just the output
items.summary: Ask for the task in five different phrasings and see if the skill actually loads.
items.detail: Most skill failures are discovery failures — the body is fine, it just never runs. Start fresh sessions, phrase the request the way a real user would (including badly), and watch whether it fires. Then fix the description, not the body.
items.snippet:
# fresh session, five phrasings
"roast this" · "is this pitch any good" · "feedback on my draft"
"be honest about this press release" · "would a journalist open this"
